title: [Synthetic fixture] Insulin resistance and beta-cell function in type 2 diabetes
abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus is characterised by reduced responsiveness of muscle, liver and fat tissue to insulin, together with a progressive decline in the ability of pancreatic beta cells to secrete enough insulin. When cells respond poorly to insulin, less glucose is taken up from the blood and the liver continues to release glucose, so blood glucose concentrations rise. Over time the beta cells must work harder, and their capacity to compensate can fail. This text describes the textbook two-part model of impaired insulin action plus impaired insulin secretion.

title: [Synthetic fixture] Physical activity, body weight and glycaemic control
abstract: Regular physical activity increases glucose uptake by skeletal muscle through insulin-dependent and insulin-independent pathways. Body weight reduction in people with excess adiposity is associated with improved insulin sensitivity. Dietary patterns that limit rapidly absorbed carbohydrates produce smaller rises in blood glucose after meals. This synthetic summary does not report any trial and gives no clinical recommendations.

title: [Synthetic fixture] Chronic hyperglycaemia and long-term vascular complications
abstract: Persistently elevated blood glucose can damage small blood vessels in the retina, kidneys and peripheral nerves, leading to retinopathy, nephropathy and neuropathy. Mechanisms proposed in textbooks include accumulation of advanced glycation end products and increased oxidative stress in vascular cells. Large blood vessels are also affected, which increases the risk of cardiovascular disease.

title: [Synthetic fixture] Life cycle of Plasmodium parasites in humans and mosquitoes
abstract: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium parasites transmitted by the bite of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes. Sporozoites travel to the liver and invade hepatocytes, where they multiply and are released as merozoites. Merozoites then invade red blood cells and multiply again; the bursting of infected red blood cells releases more merozoites and is associated with the cyclical fever characteristic of the disease. Some parasites develop into gametocytes that can be taken up by a mosquito.

title: [Synthetic fixture] Bed nets and indoor spraying as vector control
abstract: Vector control reduces contact between people and mosquitoes. Insecticide-treated bed nets act as both a physical barrier and a chemical one that kills or repels mosquitoes that land on them. Indoor residual spraying treats the inner walls of houses with insecticide. Insecticide resistance in mosquito populations is a recognised challenge for these methods.

title: [Synthetic fixture] Sickle cell trait and susceptibility to severe malaria
abstract: Individuals who carry one copy of the sickle haemoglobin variant, known as sickle cell trait, are generally less likely to develop severe malaria than individuals without the variant. Proposed explanations include impaired parasite growth inside red blood cells that contain sickle haemoglobin and enhanced removal of infected cells. This textbook-level association is a classic example of balanced selection.

title: [Synthetic fixture] Airway inflammation and narrowing in asthma
abstract: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disease of the airways. Exposure to triggers such as allergens or viral infections can cause airway smooth muscle to contract, the airway lining to swell, and mucus production to increase; together these narrow the airways and make breathing difficult. Eosinophils, mast cells and T helper 2 lymphocytes are among the immune cells commonly implicated in allergic asthma.

title: [Synthetic fixture] Mechanisms of bronchodilators and inhaled corticosteroids
abstract: Short-acting beta-2 agonists relax airway smooth muscle by activating beta-2 adrenergic receptors, which widens the airways within minutes. Inhaled corticosteroids reduce airway inflammation by altering gene expression in immune and airway cells, an effect that develops over days to weeks. This synthetic description explains drug mechanisms only and is not a treatment guideline.

title: [Synthetic fixture] Allergen sensitisation and immunoglobulin E in allergic asthma
abstract: In allergic asthma, exposure to an allergen can lead to production of allergen-specific immunoglobulin E (IgE). IgE binds to receptors on mast cells; later allergen exposure cross-links the bound IgE and triggers release of histamine and other mediators, producing rapid airway narrowing.

title: [Synthetic fixture] Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection and granuloma formation
abstract: Tuberculosis is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, which spreads through airborne droplets. After inhalation the bacteria are engulfed by alveolar macrophages, in which they can survive. The immune system may wall off infected macrophages within structures called granulomas, which can contain the infection for long periods without clearing it completely.

title: [Synthetic fixture] Why tuberculosis therapy combines several antibiotics
abstract: Mycobacterium tuberculosis grows slowly and can exist in different metabolic states. Treatment regimens combine several antibiotics for months because a single drug would allow resistant bacteria to emerge and because different drugs act on different bacterial populations. Drug-resistant tuberculosis arises when treatment is incomplete or inappropriate.

title: [Synthetic fixture] BCG vaccination and tuberculosis prevention
abstract: The BCG vaccine is derived from a weakened strain of Mycobacterium bovis. It provides protection against severe forms of tuberculosis in young children, such as tuberculous meningitis, while its protection against pulmonary tuberculosis in adults is variable.
